quote: the, actually, location where I live in near field, they have, I I think, pretty, stringent regulations on what's allowed, but I wasn't sure if maybe somebody had the ability to navigate whether or not that's that's possible.
stewart_read: The customer raises a feasibility/regulatory question at the very start of the call. The rep never directly answers or confirms it was routed to the specialist -- he says only 'I gotcha' and moves to verify. This is a minor, low-severity gap: the customer does not resurface the concern and cooperates fully through the rest of the call, so it did not visibly cost engagement, but it was also never closed out with an explicit bridge to the specialist.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged this was standard specialist-tier content not requiring an on-the-spot answer, and the generic acknowledgment was intentional scope discipline.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to use the explicit escape hatch ('that's exactly what our specialist will look into for your area') rather than a vague acknowledgment -- even a low-stakes concern deserves a named handoff so the customer knows it hasn't been forgotten.

quote: I'm gonna I'm gonna guess the average is around $3.50,
stewart_read: The customer gives a bill figure and the rep acknowledges it factually ('Around $3.50. Okay.') then adds a seasonal comment, but never flips it into emotional leverage against the utility or ties it to savings motivation.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest missed flip on the call -- coach the rep to follow a captured bill number with a line that turns it into the reason to act, e.g., reflecting the number back as the target to beat.

quote: Yeah. You can I see an email would be would be great?
stewart_read: The customer agrees to send the bill via email with no resistance, but the rep never uses this moment to build anticipation about what the design will show him -- it's treated as a pure logistics handoff.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be intentionally holding back detail per setter-scope discipline, saving any 'what you'll see' framing for the specialist.
coaching_implication: A short forward-pulling line here ('once we get this over to design, you'll see exactly what your system could look like') would have added stickiness to the appointment before the booking friction hit.

quote: You you're talking about a phone call. Right?
stewart_read: The appointment format (in-person vs. phone) was never stated anywhere earlier in the call before the rep tried to book a slot. The customer's assumption that it would be a phone call surfaces only at the moment of booking, and this surprise appears to contribute directly to his pullback into 'we're pretty busy.' This is a schema gap in this instance: Ion's button_up protocol specifies stating the appointment channel, and it was skipped until it caused friction.
alternative_hypothesis: The customer may have pulled back regardless of format, purely due to genuine weekend/travel conflicts unrelated to the phone/in-person surprise.
coaching_implication: State the appointment channel (in-person specialist visit) early and plainly before offering times, so the customer isn't reconciling a new expectation at the exact moment he's asked to commit to a slot.

quote: Actually, we're we're pretty busy over the weekend. Tell you what, can I look at my schedule? And then when I email you the AEP information, I'll let you know, like, when I'm free, like because I I travel a handful for work, and then our family's gonna be out of town.
stewart_read: The customer bundles two open items together -- sending the bill AND telling the rep his availability -- into a single deferred action, with no date or time attached. The rep accepts this bundling without trying to pin down even a tentative window (e.g., 'sometime next week, morning or afternoon?').
coaching_implication: When a customer offers to follow up with availability, the rep should still try to narrow it on the call -- 'no problem, and just so I can hold something provisional, are early or late next week better for you?' -- rather than leaving the entire scheduling question open-ended.

quote: Okay. Okay. Awesome. That works. Great. Yeah. Well, appreciate your time, Tom. I'll just look out for your email, and then we can kinda just go from there.
stewart_read: The call closes with no confirmed date, no confirmed time, no recap of next steps, and no verbal handshake. 'We can kinda just go from there' is a passive close with no rep-owned commitment.
coaching_implication: Even in a genuinely fluid scheduling situation, the rep should own the next step explicitly: 'I'll follow up with you Monday once I have your bill and we can lock in a time that week' -- something concrete the rep is accountable for, not a vague wait-and-see.

quote: Yeah. Great. Yeah. Well, I got it pulled up here on Google Maps and a very beautiful home, by the way.
stewart_read: A small, genuine personalization touch inserted naturally into the verify flow -- this is the kind of neighbor-like energy the schema calls for rather than a mechanical Q&A.
coaching_implication: Reinforce this behavior -- it's a positive example of weaving rapport into verify rather than checklisting it.
